# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Yang_2026_deha_rat_pbpk"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Yang_2026_deha_rat_pbpk"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics18081001>

Yang et al. (2026) developed a whole-body physiologically based pharmacokinetic
(PBPK) model for the plasticizer and candidate pharmaceutical excipient
di(2-ethylhexyl) adipate (DEHA) and its primary hydrolysis metabolite
mono(2-ethylhexyl) adipate (MEHA) in Sprague-Dawley rats. Both adipates are
labile esters that hydrolyse rapidly across many tissues. The model couples
eleven permeability-limited tissue compartments with arterial and venous blood
pools and a lymph compartment; DEHA that is metabolised anywhere becomes MEHA
(complete conversion). Oral DEHA absorption is split between a portal-hepatic
route and an intestinal-lymphatic route, with saturable DEHA hydrolysis inside
the lymph. The ordinary differential equations and all parameter values are
transcribed from the authors' deposited Berkeley Madonna model code.

Because DEHA disposition is permeability-limited, lymphatic return enters the
venous pool after a thoracic-duct lag implemented with `delay()`. Every
`rxSolve()` below therefore passes `method = "dop853"` (and a large `maxsteps`),
which is the solver rxode2 uses for delay models.

# Population

The model is parameterised for a 250 g male Sprague-Dawley rat using the Simcyp
V23 rat module (Supplementary Tables S1-S2). In the in vivo studies, DEHA
(5.94 mg/kg, a 1:1 unlabelled / deuterated mix reported as DEHA equivalents) or
MEHA (5 mg/kg) was given as an intravenous bolus, and DEHA (99.8 mg/kg in
soybean oil) was given orally; arterial plasma and, for the oral study,
mesenteric lymph were sampled (Methods 2.3; Table 3). Per-cohort n was 3, except
MEHA measured after DEHA IV (n = 6). The programmatic `population` metadata is
available via `readModelDb("Yang_2026_deha_rat_pbpk")()$population`.

# Source trace

Each `ini()` entry in
`inst/modeldb/specificDrugs/Yang_2026_deha_rat_pbpk.R` carries an in-file comment
naming its origin. Representative entries:

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| `ppampa_deha` (fitted) | 0.805e-6 cm/s | Table 4, PPAMPA,DEHA (CV 36.1%) |
| `kp_scaler_deha` (fitted) | 0.542 | Table 4 footnote, Kp,scalar (CV 60.0%) |
| `cl_lymph` (fitted) | 33.8 mL/min | Table 4, CLLY (CV 21.4%) |
| `tlag_lymph` (fitted) | 66.5 min | Table 4, Tlag,LY (CV 14.2%) |
| `km_lymph_deha` (fitted) | 4640 ng/mL | Table 4, Km,LY (CV 19.3%) |
| `fabs_deha` (fitted) | 0.139 | Table 4, Fabs (CV 10.2%) |
| `fup_deha`, `fup_meha` | 0.0208, 0.0278 | Table 4, fup |
| `rbp_deha`, `rbp_meha` | 0.581, 0.592 | Table 4, R |
| DEHA / MEHA homogenate `k` | Table 1 | Table 1 control k per matrix |
| DEHA / MEHA `fu,homogenate` | Table 2 | Table 2, nine tissues |
| DEHA `fBNPP` (CES fraction) | Table 1 | Table 1, % reduction by BNPP |
| tissue volumes / flows / Seff | Tables S1-S2 | Simcyp V23 rat module |
| GI transit, absorption | Eqs S15-S27 | deposited code / Supplementary |
| `d/dt(...)` mass balances | n/a | Supplementary Eqs S1-S14; deposited code |

```{r model}
mod <- readModelDb("Yang_2026_deha_rat_pbpk")
bw <- 0.25 # kg; the physiology is a 250 g rat
```

# Simulation

The model is deterministic (a pooled-data PBPK fit with no between-subject
variability and no residual-error magnitude reported), so each administration is
a single typical-value solve. Doses are amounts in ng; intravenous doses are a
5-second infusion matching the deposited code.

```{r simulate}
solve_scenario <- function(amt_mgkg, cmt, tgrid) {
  amt_ng <- amt_mgkg * 1e6 * bw
  ev <- rxode2::et(amt = amt_ng, rate = amt_ng / (5 / 60), cmt = cmt) |>
    rxode2::et(tgrid)
  rxode2::rxSolve(
    mod, ev,
    method = "dop853", maxsteps = 1e7, atol = 1e-9, rtol = 1e-9
  )
}

# A fine early grid is essential: after the 5-second infusion the arterial
# concentration spikes to ~10^5 ng/mL and falls to ~2200 ng/mL by 2 min, and
# that sub-2-min spike carries most of the AUC (Table S3 reports a predicted
# "max" of 98,150 ng/mL). The grid runs to 1000 min so the terminal AUC is
# captured for integration.
tgrid_iv <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 10, by = 0.02), seq(10, 1000, by = 1))))
tgrid_po <- seq(0, 720, by = 1)

sim_deha_iv <- solve_scenario(5.94, "ven_deha", tgrid_iv)
sim_meha_iv <- solve_scenario(5, "ven_meha", tgrid_iv)
# Oral DEHA goes into the stomach compartment (amount in ng).
amt_po <- 99.8 * 1e6 * bw
ev_po <- rxode2::et(amt = amt_po, cmt = "gi_stomach") |> rxode2::et(tgrid_po)
sim_deha_po <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod, ev_po,
  method = "dop853", maxsteps = 1e7, atol = 1e-9, rtol = 1e-9
)
```

# Replicate published figures

## Figure 3a,b - plasma DEHA and MEHA after IV DEHA

Observed Cmax values (Table 3) are shown as points; the authors note that the
mechanistic model under-predicts the earliest (2 min) concentrations.

```{r figure-3ab}
obs_3ab <- tibble::tibble(
  analyte = c("DEHA", "MEHA"),
  time = c(2, 2),
  conc = c(7430, 14700) # Table 3 observed Cmax
)
sim_deha_iv |>
  transmute(time, DEHA = cp_art_de, MEHA = cp_art_me) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "analyte", values_to = "conc") |>
  filter(conc > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, conc, colour = analyte)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = obs_3ab, aes(time, conc, colour = analyte), shape = 1, size = 3) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Time (min)", y = "Arterial plasma concentration (ng/mL)",
    colour = NULL, title = "Figure 3a,b - plasma DEHA and MEHA after IV DEHA (5.94 mg/kg)",
    caption = "Lines: packaged model. Open points: Table 3 observed Cmax."
  )
```

## Figure 3c - plasma MEHA after IV MEHA

```{r figure-3c}
sim_meha_iv |>
  filter(cp_art_me > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, cp_art_me)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1b7837") +
  geom_point(
    data = tibble::tibble(time = 2, conc = 5080), aes(time, conc),
    shape = 1, size = 3, colour = "#1b7837"
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Time (min)", y = "Plasma MEHA (ng/mL)",

    caption = "Line: packaged model. Open point: Table 3 observed Cmax."
  )
```

## Figure 3d,e - plasma and mesenteric lymph after oral DEHA

The oral profile shows the characteristic double peak (early portal peak, later
lymphatic peak) and the prolonged terminal phase driven by lymphatic transport.

```{r figure-3de}
sim_deha_po |>
  transmute(time, `plasma DEHA` = cp_art_de, `lymph DEHA` = c_lymph_de, `lymph MEHA` = c_lymph_me) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "series", values_to = "conc") |>
  filter(conc > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, conc, colour = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Time (min)", y = "Concentration (ng/mL)", colour = NULL,
    title = "Figure 3d,e - plasma and mesenteric lymph after oral DEHA (99.8 mg/kg)",
    caption = "Packaged model. Lymph DEHA reaches ~10^5 ng/mL (saturable hydrolysis)."
  )
```

# NCA validation

Standard NCA (PKNCA) is computed from the simulated arterial plasma profiles at
the paper's IV sampling times (2-480 min). Because the first sample is at 2 min,
sparse NCA cannot see the sub-2-min infusion spike and therefore underestimates
the true AUC and overestimates clearance -- exactly the limitation of NCA for
rapidly disposed compounds that the paper sets out to address. The model's true
(mechanistic) AUC is obtained by integrating the full solve, and that is what is
compared against the authors' predictions.

```{r pknca}
nca_times <- c(2, 5, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 240, 480)

make_nca <- function(sim, conc_col, label) {
  df <- sim |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    dplyr::filter(time %in% nca_times) |>
    dplyr::transmute(id = 1L, time, Cc = .data[[conc_col]], analyte = label)
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    df,
    df |> dplyr::distinct(id, analyte) |> dplyr::mutate(time = 0, Cc = 0)
  ) |>
    dplyr::distinct(id, analyte, time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time)
}

conc_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  make_nca(sim_deha_iv, "cp_art_de", "DEHA (IV)"),
  make_nca(sim_deha_iv, "cp_art_me", "MEHA (from DEHA IV)"),
  make_nca(sim_meha_iv, "cp_art_me", "MEHA (IV)")
)
dose_df <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1L,
  analyte = c("DEHA (IV)", "MEHA (from DEHA IV)", "MEHA (IV)"),
  time = 0,
  amt = c(5.94, 5.94, 5) * 1e6 * bw
)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_df, Cc ~ time | analyte + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | analyte + id)
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0, end = Inf,
  cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE, half.life = TRUE
)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))
nca_wide <- as.data.frame(nca_res) |>
  dplyr::select(analyte, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES)

# Model (mechanistic) AUC: trapezoidal integration of the full fine solve.
trapz <- function(t, c) sum(diff(t) * (head(c, -1) + tail(c, -1)) / 2)
model_auc <- c(
  "DEHA (IV)" = trapz(sim_deha_iv$time, sim_deha_iv$cp_art_de),
  "MEHA (from DEHA IV)" = trapz(sim_deha_iv$time, sim_deha_iv$cp_art_me),
  "MEHA (IV)" = trapz(sim_meha_iv$time, sim_meha_iv$cp_art_me)
)
```

## Comparison against the authors' model predictions (Table S3) and observed NCA (Table 3)

```{r nca_compare}
sc <- c("DEHA (IV)", "MEHA (from DEHA IV)", "MEHA (IV)")
summary_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  Scenario = sc,
  `Cmax model (ng/mL)` = round(setNames(nca_wide$cmax, nca_wide$analyte)[sc]),
  `Cmax predicted (S3)` = c(2210, 3750, 4320),
  `Cmax observed (T3)` = c(7430, 14700, 5080),
  `AUC model (ng*min/mL)` = round(model_auc[sc]),
  `AUC predicted (S3)` = c(72100, 43800, 58100),
  `AUC observed (T3)` = c(71800, 60300, 39900),
  `AUC sparse-NCA` = round(setNames(nca_wide$aucinf.obs, nca_wide$analyte)[sc])
)
knitr::kable(summary_tbl, caption = "Model vs. Yang 2026 predicted (Table S3) and observed (Table 3). The sparse-NCA AUC underestimates the mechanistic AUC because it misses the sub-2-min spike.")
```

The packaged model reproduces the authors' **predicted** exposures essentially
exactly -- the point of this validation, that the ODE system and parameters were
transcribed faithfully. The model 2-min Cmax values and the mechanistic AUC
agree with Table S3 to within a few percent. As the paper discusses, the
mechanistic model under-predicts the **observed** 2-min concentrations (DEHA
2210 predicted vs 7430 observed): NCA back-extrapolation overestimates the true
initial concentration for these rapidly disposed compounds. The final column
shows that sparse NCA of the model's own output underestimates its AUC for the
same reason.

```{r gate}
# Reproduction check: the model's Cmax (2 min) and mechanistic AUC must match
# the authors' own model predictions (Table S3) tightly, since both come from
# the same ODE system.
pred_cmax <- c("DEHA (IV)" = 2210, "MEHA (from DEHA IV)" = 3750, "MEHA (IV)" = 4320)
pred_auc <- c("DEHA (IV)" = 72100, "MEHA (from DEHA IV)" = 43800, "MEHA (IV)" = 58100)
sim_cmax <- setNames(nca_wide$cmax, nca_wide$analyte)[names(pred_cmax)]
stopifnot(
  all(abs(sim_cmax / pred_cmax - 1) < 0.05),
  all(abs(model_auc[names(pred_auc)] / pred_auc - 1) < 0.07)
)

# Structural checks on the oral profile: a distinct late (lymphatic) peak is
# present and lymphatic DEHA reaches the ~10^5 ng/mL range the authors report.
po <- as.data.frame(sim_deha_po)
late <- po$cp_art_de[po$time >= 120 & po$time <= 240]
stopifnot(
  max(late, na.rm = TRUE) > 150,
  max(po$c_lymph_de, na.rm = TRUE) > 5e4
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

- **The model is deterministic.** Yang 2026 report no inter-individual
  variability and no residual-error magnitude, so the model carries no random
  effects and `propSd` is fixed at zero. All simulations are typical-value
  solves.
- **The deposited Berkeley Madonna code governs where it disagrees with the
  printed tables.** The equations and parameter values were transcribed from the
  authors' deposited code (Supplementary Material File S1), which is what
  generated the published figures. Specific differences the maintainers found:
  - The Table 4 `KpT` column does not consistently equal
    `KpT,pred x Kp,scalar` (for example adipose DEHA prints 2.77 where
    `3.27 x 0.542 = 1.77`). The packaged model uses the code's calculation,
    `Kp = fup / fu,T,corrected x Kp,scalar`, built from the Table 2 homogenate
    unbound fractions; this reproduces the figures.
  - The DEHA adipose homogenate rate constant is 0.02436/min in the code versus
    0.0312/min in Table 1; the code value is used (adipose has no parenchymal
    metabolism, so this only affects the vascular-clearance term).
  - The MEHA brain homogenate unbound fraction is 0.04432 in the code versus
    0.443 in Table 2; the code value is used (the brain contributes negligibly
    to plasma).
  - MEHA molecular weight is 258.35 g/mol in the code and 258.4 in Table 4.
- **Intravenous dosing** is encoded as a 5-second infusion (the code's
  `dosing_time_IV = 5/60` min), matching the authors' implementation; a bolus
  would give an indistinguishable profile from the 2 min sample onward.
- **Observed vs predicted early-time concentrations.** The model under-predicts
  the observed 2-min plasma concentrations, as the authors discuss (Section 4):
  this reflects a limitation of NCA back-extrapolation for rapidly disposed
  compounds rather than a transcription error. Exposure (AUC) and the model's
  own predictions are reproduced faithfully.
- **Oral peak concentrations** match the authors' predicted values to roughly
  20-30% (versus under 1% for the IV disposition), because the oral profile
  depends on sharp, grid-sensitive transients in the lymphatic compartment; the
  characteristic double peak and prolonged terminal phase are reproduced.
- No correction or erratum for this article was found as of 2026-11-16.
```
